stimuli.title: From Running Machine to Freedom Machine
stimuli.source: Original passage written for KCE GED Prep.
stimuli.html:
[1] In June 1817, a German inventor named Karl Drais set out along a road near the city of Mannheim on a strange wooden contraption. It had two wheels in a line, a padded seat, and a bar for steering, but no pedals. The rider sat astride the frame and pushed against the ground with his feet, gliding between strides. Drais called his invention a Laufmaschine, or “running machine.” In England, where copies soon appeared, it was nicknamed the “dandy horse.”

[2] Why would anyone want a horse with no legs? Some historians have suggested an answer. In 1815, a massive volcanic eruption in what is now Indonesia threw ash high into the atmosphere, and the following year was so cold in parts of Europe that it became known as “the year without a summer.” Crops failed, and the oats used to feed horses grew scarce and expensive. A vehicle that needed no feed, the argument goes, must have seemed especially appealing. Other historians are less certain. They point out that no known writing by Drais links his invention to the poor harvests, and that the theory rests mainly on the timing of the two events.

[3] The running machine turned out to be a short-lived fad, and the next major step did not come for decades. In France in the 1860s, builders attached pedals directly to the front wheel. Now a rider could keep moving forward without touching the ground. These machines, called velocipedes, had heavy wooden wheels with iron rims. On cobblestone streets they gave such a jarring ride that English speakers called them “boneshakers.”

[4] Because the pedals turned the front wheel directly, each full turn of the pedals moved the machine forward exactly one turn of that wheel. Builders soon realized that a larger front wheel would carry a rider farther with every push. By the 1870s, front wheels had grown as tall as five feet. These high-wheelers were fast, but they were also dangerous. The rider sat high above the front wheel, and a stone or rut in the road could stop the wheel suddenly and pitch the rider headfirst over the handlebars. Riding one took athletic skill, nerve, and money, so most riders were young men of some wealth.

[5] The design that changed everything appeared in England in 1885. John Kemp Starley's Rover “safety bicycle” had two wheels of similar size and a chain that linked the pedals to the rear wheel. By using gears of different sizes, the chain allowed a modest wheel to cover as much ground with each turn of the pedals as a giant one had. Riders sat low enough to put their feet down when they stopped. In 1888, John Boyd Dunlop received a patent for an air-filled rubber tire, and soon such tires were softening the ride. The bicycle had become something almost anyone could learn to use.

[6] In the 1890s, the United States went bicycle crazy. Hundreds of companies were making bicycles, and as prices fell, the machines spread from wealthy sportsmen to clerks, factory workers, and students. The change was especially dramatic for women. A woman on a bicycle could travel on her own, without a driver or an escort, and many riders traded heavy, floor-length skirts for shorter skirts or loose trousers called bloomers. In an 1896 newspaper interview, the women's rights leader Susan B. Anthony declared that bicycling “has done more to emancipate women than anything else in the world.”

[7] The bicycle shaped other inventions as well. Two brothers in Dayton, Ohio, Wilbur and Orville Wright, opened a bicycle shop in 1892 and began building their own models a few years later. The skills they learned there, from working with light frames and chains to understanding how a rider keeps balance on a moving machine, helped them build the airplane they flew in 1903.

[8] More than a century later, the basic shape of Starley's safety bicycle has hardly changed. A machine that began as a substitute for the horse became, for millions of people, a first taste of independence.

stimuli.title: Endgame
stimuli.source: Original fiction written for KCE GED Prep.
stimuli.html:
[1] The chessboard had lived on the kitchen table for as long as Sofia could remember. It was a cheap folding board with a crease down the middle, and one of the white pawns had been replaced years ago by a blue button. Her grandfather had taught her to play on it when she was seven. When she was eight, she had beaten him for the first time, and he had laughed so hard he had to take off his glasses.

[2] Now she was fifteen, and she had not touched the board in four months.

[3] That was when Mateo, who was ten, had beaten her. Not once, but three games in a row on a rainy Saturday, his feet swinging under the table, humming to himself while he moved his knight through her defenses like a cat crossing a yard. After the third game, she had said she was bored of chess, and she had gone to her room and shut the door harder than she meant to.

[4] Since then, Mateo had joined the chess club at the library, and their grandfather drove him there every Thursday. Sofia found reasons to be busy. She told herself she had outgrown the game.

[5] The city tournament was held in a school gym that smelled of floor wax and orange peels. Sofia had come only because her mother needed someone to sit with Mateo while she worked a double shift. She sat in the bleachers with her phone, not looking at the long rows of tables where children bent over their boards in silence.

[6] In the fourth round, Mateo played a tall boy in a team jacket who slapped the clock after each move as if it had insulted him. Sofia did not mean to watch. But from the bleachers, she could see the board. By the twentieth move, she felt a small, cold drop in her stomach: Mateo had left his queen unguarded. Three moves later, the tall boy saw it, too.

[7] Mateo did not cry at the table. He shook the boy's hand, the way their grandfather had taught both of them, and wrote the result on his score sheet in careful block letters. Then he walked straight past the bleachers and out the side door.

[8] Sofia found him sitting on the curb by the bike rack, holding the score sheet in both hands.

[9] “I saw the queen,” he said, without looking up. “Right after I moved. I saw it, and I couldn't take it back.”

[10] She sat down next to him. The concrete was cold through her jeans. For a while neither of them said anything.

[11] “Abuelo says the game remembers everything,” Mateo said finally. “Every move stays on the board.”

[12] “Abuelo says a lot of things.” She bumped his shoulder with hers. “He also says the best players lose more games than anybody, because they play more games than anybody.”

[13] Mateo almost smiled. “You haven't played in four months.”

[14] “I know.” She looked down at the score sheet, at the neat columns of moves that led, one by one, to the mistake. “Show me where it went wrong. Then show me what you'd do instead.”

[15] That night, the folding board came back out on the kitchen table. Mateo set up the pieces, blue button and all, and turned the board so that Sofia had white.

stimuli.title: Let Teenagers Sleep: Start High School Later
stimuli.source: By Dr. Andrea Lin, pediatrician. Original passage written for KCE GED Prep.
stimuli.html:
Every weekday, millions of American teenagers drag themselves out of bed before sunrise to catch a bus for a school day that may begin as early as 7:15 a.m. We tell them to go to bed earlier. The science says that advice misses the point. High schools should start no earlier than 8:30 a.m.

During puberty, the body's internal clock shifts. Teenagers begin releasing melatonin, the hormone that makes people sleepy, later in the evening than younger children or adults do. As a result, many teenagers have difficulty falling asleep before about 11:00 p.m., no matter how early they go to bed. Sleep experts recommend that teens get 8 to 10 hours of sleep a night. A student who falls asleep at 11:00 and wakes at 6:00 to catch a 6:45 bus gets seven hours at most. In 2014, the American Academy of Pediatrics reviewed this research and recommended that middle and high schools start at 8:30 a.m. or later.

Districts that have made the change have seen results. When the Lakeview School District moved its high school start time from 7:30 to 8:35 a.m., researchers from a nearby university surveyed students before and after the change. Students reported sleeping an average of 34 minutes more per night. Over the next two years, first-period attendance rose, the number of students reported for falling asleep in class dropped by nearly half, and car crashes involving teen drivers in the district fell by 16 percent. Similar improvements have been reported in other districts around the country.

Critics worry about cost and convenience. Changing bus routes can cost money, and after-school sports and jobs may end later. These concerns are real, but they can be managed. Many districts have solved the bus problem by having elementary schools, whose younger students naturally wake earlier, start first. Practices can be shifted, and lights can be added to fields. None of these challenges outweighs the health and safety of students.

We would never schedule a team to compete at the hour when its players' bodies are least able to perform. Yet that is exactly what early start times do to learning. Schools exist to help students succeed. Letting them start the day awake is a simple place to begin.

stimuli.title: Later Start Times Would Create More Problems Than They Solve
stimuli.source: By Dennis Hale, parent and local business owner. Original passage written for KCE GED Prep.
stimuli.html:
Everyone wants teenagers to be healthy and well rested. But pushing back the start of the high school day is an expensive, disruptive answer to a problem that families can solve at home.

The real reason teenagers are tired is not the bell schedule. It is their phones. My own son used to stay up past midnight scrolling through videos, then complain that school started too early. When we started collecting phones at 10:00 p.m., he began falling asleep on time. If every parent set rules like ours, students would get plenty of sleep without the school changing anything.

A later start would also cost money our district does not have. Our buses run three routes every morning, one each for the high school, the middle school, and the elementary schools. Changing the schedule could mean buying more buses and hiring more drivers. A transportation official in a neighboring district told me that such a change could cost as much as $1 million a year. That money should go into classrooms, not buses.

Later start times also mean later end times. If school lets out at 3:45 instead of 2:30, practices and games will run into the evening, and student athletes will get home late to start their homework, losing the very sleep the change was supposed to give them. Many teenagers also work after school to help their families. Employers will not wait for them.

Parents in our community agree with me. At last month's school board meeting, nine of the eleven parents who spoke opposed the change.

Finally, school is supposed to prepare young people for adult life. Most jobs start at 8:00 or 9:00 in the morning, and no boss is going to change the schedule because an employee is tired. If we let teenagers sleep in now, we will only make it harder for them to adjust when they enter the working world.

Instead of rearranging every family's schedule, we should teach students good sleep habits and expect parents to enforce them. That solution costs nothing.

stimuli.title: Cities Built by Animals
stimuli.source: Original passage written for KCE GED Prep.
stimuli.html:
[1] From the deck of a boat, a coral reef can look like a garden of colorful rocks. Up close, it is something stranger: a structure built over thousands of years by animals, most of them smaller than a pencil eraser.

[2] Those animals are coral polyps. Each polyp is a soft-bodied creature with a tube-shaped body and a ring of stinging tentacles around its mouth, a close relative of jellyfish and sea anemones. A polyp draws minerals from seawater and uses them to build a hard cup of limestone around its base. When the polyp dies, the cup remains, and new polyps build on top of it. Layer by layer, generation after generation, millions of these tiny skeletons add up to a reef. Many reef-building corals grow less than an inch a year, which means that a large reef may be thousands of years old.

[3] Corals could not build at this scale on their own. Living inside the tissues of most reef-building corals are microscopic algae. Like plants, the algae use sunlight to make food through photosynthesis, and they share much of that food with the coral, in some species as much as 90 percent of the energy the coral needs. In return, the coral gives the algae a protected home and supplies some of the raw materials they use. The algae also give many corals their brilliant greens, browns, and purples. Because the algae depend on sunlight, most reefs grow in shallow, clear water in warm tropical seas.

[4] The reefs that result are among the richest habitats on Earth. Although coral reefs cover less than 1 percent of the ocean floor, scientists estimate that they support about a quarter of all known marine species. Fish shelter among the corals, feed on the creatures that live there, and lay their eggs nearby. People benefit as well. Hundreds of millions of people depend on reefs for fish to eat or for income from fishing and tourism. Reefs also act as natural breakwaters: by slowing waves before they reach shore, a healthy reef protects coastal towns from erosion and storm damage.

[5] Yet the partnership that builds a reef is fragile. Corals live close to the upper limit of the temperatures they can bear. When the water stays even 1 degree Celsius (about 2 degrees Fahrenheit) warmer than the usual summer maximum for several weeks, the partnership begins to break down. The stressed corals expel their algae. Without the algae, the coral's tissue becomes nearly transparent, and the white limestone skeleton shows through. This is called coral bleaching. A bleached coral is not dead, but it is starving. If temperatures return to normal soon enough, the algae can return and the coral can recover. If the heat lasts too long, the coral dies, and seaweed may soon cover its skeleton.

[6] As ocean temperatures have risen, bleaching has become more frequent. In the past, mass bleaching events, in which corals across a wide region bleach at the same time, were rare. Now they occur often enough that many reefs have little time to recover between them. Australia's Great Barrier Reef, the largest reef system in the world, has experienced several mass bleaching events since 2016.

[7] Heat is not the only threat. Pollution running off the land clouds the water and blocks sunlight. Overfishing removes fish that graze on seaweed, allowing it to crowd out young corals. And as the ocean absorbs carbon dioxide from the air, seawater becomes slightly more acidic, which makes it harder for corals to build their skeletons.

[8] Scientists stress that reefs can still recover if they are given the chance. Reducing local threats such as pollution and overfishing gives corals the best odds of surviving the heat waves that are already coming. Over the long term, though, most researchers agree that the survival of the world's reefs depends on slowing the warming of the oceans themselves.

stimuli.title: Can We Replant a Reef?
stimuli.source: Original passage written for KCE GED Prep. Table data are illustrative.
stimuli.html:
[1] On a sandy patch of seafloor, rows of plastic pipe frames rise from the bottom like small, leafless trees. Hanging from their branches are hundreds of finger-sized pieces of living coral. This is a coral nursery, and the people who tend it hope it can help bring damaged reefs back to life.

[2] The method takes advantage of the way some corals grow. When a branch of certain corals breaks off, the fragment can survive and grow into a new colony. Restoration teams collect small fragments from healthy corals, hang them in nurseries where they can be watched and cleaned, and wait. In a nursery, a fast-growing branching coral can grow to many times its original size within a year. The teams then “outplant” the young corals, attaching them to a damaged reef with marine cement or ties.

[3] Supporters point out that restoration can work quickly in small areas. Divers who visit a successful site may see thickets of branching coral where there was bare rubble only a few years before. Restoration projects also give local communities and visitors a direct way to help, and they let scientists study which corals best survive heat. Some teams now look for heat-tolerant corals, colonies that stayed healthy during a bleaching event, and grow more of them on purpose.

[4] Critics do not argue that restoration is useless, but they warn against expecting too much from it. Even the largest projects have replanted only a tiny fraction of the reef area that has been lost. Outplanted corals face the same warm water as the reef around them, and a single severe marine heat wave can wipe out much of a nursery's work. Critics compare restoration without action on ocean warming to mopping the floor while the sink is still overflowing.

[5] Results from one sample project show both sides of the debate. The table below follows 1,000 coral fragments that a team outplanted on a damaged reef.

Survival of 1,000 Outplanted Coral Fragments at a Sample Restoration Site

Time after outplantingFragments still alivePercent of original 1,000
1 year82082%
2 years71071%
3 years (a marine heat wave struck during this year)29029%
4 years26026%

[6] Most scientists see restoration as one tool among several: a way to buy time for reefs while the larger work of reducing pollution, managing fishing, and slowing ocean warming goes on.

items.prompt: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the passage?
options: The running machine was invented because a volcanic eruption made horse feed scarce.
Through a series of design changes, the bicycle grew from a novelty into a practical machine that gave many people new independence.
The high-wheeler was the most important bicycle design because it was the fastest.
The Wright brothers' bicycle shop was the most important result of the bicycle boom.
items.explain:
The passage traces the bicycle from the pedal-less running machine (paragraph 1) through the velocipede and high-wheeler (paragraphs 3–4) to the safety bicycle that “almost anyone could learn to use” (paragraph 5), then shows its effects on ordinary riders, especially women (paragraph 6). The conclusion says the machine became “a first taste of independence” for millions.

The volcano theory is presented as uncertain (paragraph 2). The high-wheeler is described as dangerous and replaced, not as the most important design. The Wright brothers are one example in paragraph 7, not the central idea.
why: Paragraph 2 presents the volcano theory as uncertain, noting that "other historians are less certain." It is one detail, not the central idea.
Paragraph 4 calls the high-wheeler dangerous, and paragraph 5 says the safety bicycle was "the design that changed everything."
The Wright brothers appear only in paragraph 7 as one example of the bicycle's influence, not as the passage's main point.

items.prompt: Paragraph 2 is shown below. Click the sentence that gives a reason to doubt the theory that the “year without a summer” inspired the running machine.
spans: Why would anyone want a horse with no legs?
Some historians have suggested an answer.

In 1815, a massive volcanic eruption in what is now Indonesia threw ash high into the atmosphere, and the following year was so cold in parts of Europe that it became known as “the year without a summer.”
Crops failed, and the oats used to feed horses grew scarce and expensive.
A vehicle that needed no feed, the argument goes, must have seemed especially appealing.
They point out that no known writing by Drais links his invention to the poor harvests, and that the theory rests mainly on the timing of the two events.
items.explain:
The last sentence gives the actual reasons for doubt: no known writing by Drais connects his invention to the harvests, and the theory “rests mainly on the timing of the two events.” Two events happening close together does not prove that one caused the other.

“Other historians are less certain” announces that there is doubt, but it does not give a reason. The earlier sentences present the theory itself.
items.why: The most common wrong click is "Other historians are less certain," which announces doubt but gives no reason. The last sentence gives the reasons: no writing by Drais links the invention to the harvests, and the theory rests only on timing.

items.prompt: As it is used in paragraph 3, the word jarring most nearly means—
options: rough and jolting
loud and distracting
slow and tiring
sudden and surprising
items.explain:
The velocipedes had “heavy wooden wheels with iron rims” and rode on “cobblestone streets,” and people called them “boneshakers.” All of these clues describe a ride that shook and jolted the rider, so jarring means rough and jolting.

Jarring can describe a harsh sound in other sentences, but nothing in this paragraph is about noise; the nickname “boneshakers” points to shaking.
why: Jarring can describe a harsh sound, but paragraph 3 is about shaking: iron-rimmed wheels on cobblestones and the nickname "boneshakers."
Nothing in paragraph 3 says the ride was slow or tiring; the clues describe shaking and jolting.
The ride was rough the whole time, not a single sudden event; "boneshakers" points to steady shaking.

items.skill: Author's craft: purpose of a detail
items.prompt: Why does the author explain, at the start of paragraph 4, that each full turn of the pedals moved the machine forward exactly one turn of the front wheel?
options: to show that velocipedes were slower than running machines
to explain why only wealthy riders could afford high-wheelers
to describe how the chain on the safety bicycle worked
to explain why builders made the front wheels so large
items.explain:
If one turn of the pedals equals one turn of the wheel, then a bigger wheel covers more ground per turn. The next sentence makes that connection: “Builders soon realized that a larger front wheel would carry a rider farther with every push.” The detail sets up the reason front wheels grew “as tall as five feet.”

The paragraph never compares velocipedes with running machines. Wealth is mentioned at the end of the paragraph for a different reason (skill, nerve, and money). The chain belongs to the safety bicycle in paragraph 5.
why: Paragraph 4 never compares velocipedes with running machines; the detail sets up why wheels grew larger.
Wealth comes up at the end of paragraph 4 for a different reason (skill, nerve, and money), not because of the pedal-to-wheel ratio.
The chain belongs to the safety bicycle in paragraph 5. Paragraph 4 describes pedals turning the front wheel directly.

items.prompt: According to paragraph 4, which features made the high-wheeler dangerous? Select two answers.
options: The rider sat high above the front wheel.
A stone or rut in the road could suddenly stop the front wheel.
Its wooden wheels had iron rims.
It had no pedals.
Its chain could slip off the gears.
Its air-filled tires could burst.
items.explain:
Paragraph 4 says, “The rider sat high above the front wheel, and a stone or rut in the road could stop the wheel suddenly and pitch the rider headfirst over the handlebars.” The two features together explain the danger.

Iron-rimmed wooden wheels describe the velocipede (paragraph 3). Having no pedals describes the running machine (paragraph 1). The high-wheeler had no chain, and air-filled tires were not developed until 1888 (paragraph 5).
why: Iron-rimmed wooden wheels describe the velocipede in paragraph 3, not the danger of the high-wheeler.
Having no pedals describes the running machine in paragraph 1; the high-wheeler had pedals on its front wheel.
The high-wheeler had no chain; the chain came with the safety bicycle in paragraph 5.
Air-filled tires were patented in 1888 (paragraph 5), after the high-wheeler era.

items.prompt: How does paragraph 5 relate to paragraph 4?
options: Paragraph 5 gives evidence that the high-wheeler was safer than paragraph 4 suggests.
Paragraph 5 describes a competing design from France that was invented at the same time as the high-wheeler.
Paragraph 4 describes the problems of the high-wheeler, and paragraph 5 describes a design that solved them without giving up distance per pedal turn.
Paragraph 5 explains why the high-wheeler stayed more popular than the safety bicycle.
items.explain:
Paragraph 4 explains that high-wheelers were fast but dangerous because riders sat high and could be thrown forward. Paragraph 5 introduces the safety bicycle: similar-sized wheels, riders low enough to “put their feet down,” and gears that let “a modest wheel … cover as much ground with each turn of the pedals as a giant one had.” This is a problem-and-solution structure.

Paragraph 5 does not defend the high-wheeler, the safety bicycle came from England in 1885 (not France at the same time), and the passage calls the safety bicycle “the design that changed everything.”
why: Paragraph 5 does not defend the high-wheeler; it introduces a design that replaced it.
The safety bicycle came from England in 1885, not from France at the same time as the high-wheeler.
Paragraph 5 calls the safety bicycle "the design that changed everything," so it did not stay less popular.

items.prompt: Based on the passage, put these developments in the history of the bicycle in the order they happened. Drag each development into the correct position.
choices: Pedals are attached directly to the front wheel.
Karl Drais rides his running machine near Mannheim.
A chain links the pedals to the rear wheel of a bicycle with two wheels of similar size.
Front wheels grow as tall as five feet.
items.explain: (1) Drais's running machine, 1817 (paragraph 1). (2) Pedals attached to the front wheel in France, 1860s (paragraph 3). (3) High-wheelers with front wheels up to five feet tall, 1870s (paragraph 4). (4) Starley's chain-driven Rover safety bicycle, 1885 (paragraph 5).
items.why: The most common error is placing the five-foot front wheels before pedals were added. Pedals came in the 1860s (paragraph 3), and the giant wheels followed in the 1870s because pedals turned the front wheel directly (paragraph 4).

items.prompt: Why does the author include the quotation from Susan B. Anthony in paragraph 6?
options: to prove that Anthony was the first woman in the United States to ride a bicycle
to show that an important figure of the time recognized how much the bicycle changed women's lives
to argue that women today should give up floor-length skirts
to show that bicycle companies used famous people in their advertising
items.explain:
The paragraph claims that the bicycle's effect was “especially dramatic for women,” who could now “travel on her own.” Quoting a well-known women's rights leader of the 1890s, who said bicycling did “more to emancipate women than anything else,” supports that claim with the view of someone who lived through the change.

The passage never says Anthony was the first rider, gives no advice about clothing today, and does not mention advertising.
why: The passage never says Anthony was the first woman to ride; her quotation is about the bicycle's effect on women.
The passage describes clothing in the 1890s; it gives no advice about what women should wear today.
The quotation is from a newspaper interview, and the passage never mentions advertising.

items.prompt: What does paragraph 7 suggest about the Wright brothers' work in their bicycle shop?
options: It was a business they closed because it was losing money.
It convinced them that airplanes would soon replace bicycles.
It led them to build their airplane with the same chain and gears as the Rover.
It gave them practical skills that helped them solve problems in building an airplane.
items.explain:
Paragraph 7 says the skills they learned in the shop, “from working with light frames and chains to understanding how a rider keeps balance on a moving machine, helped them build the airplane they flew in 1903.”

The passage says nothing about the shop losing money or about airplanes replacing bicycles, and it never says their airplane used the Rover's parts.
why: Paragraph 7 says nothing about the shop losing money or closing.
The passage never says the Wrights thought airplanes would replace bicycles.
Paragraph 7 says skills with frames, chains, and balance helped them; it does not say the airplane used the Rover's chain and gears.

items.prompt: Based on paragraphs 3 and 4, why has Sofia stopped playing chess?
options: She was hurt and embarrassed after losing three games in a row to her younger brother.
She had truly outgrown the game and found it boring.
Her grandfather stopped playing with her so that he could coach Mateo.
She was too busy with schoolwork and a part-time job.
items.explain:
She stopped playing right after Mateo, who is five years younger, beat her “three games in a row.” She shut her door “harder than she meant to,” which shows hurt feelings, and the narrator says she only “told herself she had outgrown the game,” a hint that this excuse is not the real reason.

Her claim of boredom is what she said, not what she felt. The grandfather drives Mateo to club, but the story never says he stopped playing with Sofia. Schoolwork and a job are never mentioned; she simply “found reasons to be busy.”
why: The narrator says she only "told herself she had outgrown the game," a hint that boredom is an excuse, not the real reason.
The grandfather drives Mateo to club, but the story never says he stopped playing with Sofia.
Schoolwork and a job are never mentioned; she simply "found reasons to be busy."

items.prompt: In paragraph 3, Mateo moves his knight through Sofia's defenses “like a cat crossing a yard.” This comparison suggests that Mateo played—
options: sneakily, breaking the rules when she was not looking
nervously, as if he expected to be caught
easily and confidently, without seeming to try hard
slowly, taking a long time over every move
items.explain:
A cat crossing a yard moves calmly and at its own pace, unbothered by anything around it. Combined with the details that Mateo's feet were “swinging” and he was “humming to himself,” the comparison shows that he beat Sofia with relaxed ease.

Nothing suggests cheating or nervousness, and the relaxed image does not fit a slow, labored game.
why: A cat crossing a yard moves calmly in the open; nothing in paragraph 3 suggests cheating.
Mateo's feet were "swinging" and he was "humming," which shows ease, not nerves.
He beat her three games in a row while relaxed and humming; the image is of ease, not slow, labored play.

items.prompt: Paragraph 6 is shown below. Click the sentence that shows Sofia recognizing Mateo's mistake before his opponent does.
spans: In the fourth round, Mateo played a tall boy in a team jacket who slapped the clock after each move as if it had insulted him.
Sofia did not mean to watch.
But from the bleachers, she could see the board.
By the twentieth move, she felt a small, cold drop in her stomach: Mateo had left his queen unguarded.
Three moves later, the tall boy saw it, too.
items.explain:
At the twentieth move, Sofia feels “a small, cold drop in her stomach” because she sees that “Mateo had left his queen unguarded.” The next sentence says the opponent noticed only “three moves later,” so Sofia saw it first. This also shows that she still understands chess well.

The last sentence describes the opponent noticing, not Sofia, and the sentence about seeing the board does not mention the mistake.
items.why: The most common wrong click is the last sentence, "the tall boy saw it, too," which shows the opponent noticing. The sentence about the "small, cold drop in her stomach" at move twenty shows Sofia seeing the unguarded queen first.

items.prompt: In paragraph 7, Mateo does not cry at the table, shakes his opponent's hand, and then walks “straight past the bleachers and out the side door.” What do these actions suggest?
options: He does not care that he lost the game.
He is holding in his disappointment until he can be alone.
He believes the tall boy cheated and wants to report it.
He is going to find his grandfather to tell him the result.
items.explain:
He keeps his composure at the table (“did not cry”) and follows good manners, but then leaves the room without stopping. Outside, he sits on the curb gripping the score sheet and says, “I saw it, and I couldn't take it back.” He was upset and waited to be alone with his feelings.

His words show that he cares deeply, he blames his own move rather than his opponent, and the grandfather is not at the tournament.
why: Outside he grips the score sheet and says, "I couldn't take it back," so he cares a great deal.
Mateo blames his own move ("I saw it, and I couldn't take it back"), not the opponent.
The grandfather is not at the tournament; Sofia finds Mateo alone on the curb.

items.prompt: Which details show that both Sofia and Mateo have learned lessons from their grandfather? Select two answers.
options: Mateo shakes his opponent's hand “the way their grandfather had taught both of them.”
Sofia reminds Mateo that Abuelo says the best players lose more games than anybody.
One of the white pawns had been replaced by a blue button.
The gym smelled of floor wax and orange peels.
Mateo writes the result on his score sheet in careful block letters.
Sofia came to the tournament because her mother had to work a double shift.
items.explain:
Paragraph 7 states directly that the grandfather taught “both of them” to shake hands after a game. In paragraph 12, Sofia repeats one of Abuelo's sayings, showing that she remembers his lessons too.

The blue button, the smell of the gym, Mateo's handwriting, and the mother's shift are details of setting and plot; none of them is described as something the grandfather taught.
why: The blue button is a detail of the old board, not something the grandfather taught.
The smell of the gym is a setting detail, not a lesson from the grandfather.
The story does not say the grandfather taught Mateo to write in block letters.
The mother's double shift explains why Sofia came; it has nothing to do with the grandfather's lessons.

items.prompt: How does Sofia's attitude toward chess change over the course of the story?
options: She goes from loving tournaments to deciding never to compete again.
She goes from coaching Mateo to resenting his success.
She goes from ignoring her grandfather's advice to openly rejecting it.
She goes from avoiding the game to choosing to study and play it with Mateo again.
items.explain:
At first she “had not touched the board in four months” and “found reasons to be busy” (paragraphs 2 and 4). By the end she asks Mateo to “show me where it went wrong,” and the board “came back out on the kitchen table” (paragraphs 14–15).

The other choices reverse or invent the change. She never coached Mateo, and she quotes her grandfather's advice approvingly instead of rejecting it.
why: Sofia was avoiding chess at the start and returns to it at the end, the opposite of this choice.
Sofia never coached Mateo; at the end she asks him to show her his mistake.
Sofia quotes Abuelo's advice approvingly in paragraph 12; she does not reject it.

items.prompt: In chess, the player with the white pieces makes the first move. In paragraph 15, Mateo “turned the board so that Sofia had white.” What does this action most likely suggest?
options: He is welcoming her back to the game and offering her the first move.
He is still upset and wants her to make the first mistake.
He has forgotten which color she used to play.
He wants her to lose so that he can feel better about his own loss.
items.explain:
Sofia has just comforted Mateo and asked him to teach her from his mistake. Setting up the old board, “blue button and all,” and giving her white, the side that moves first, is a generous gesture that welcomes her back after four months away.

Mateo's mood has improved (“Mateo almost smiled”), so nothing suggests he is still upset or trying to make her lose, and nothing shows he has forgotten anything.
why: Mateo "almost smiled" and has just been comforted, so nothing suggests he is still upset.
Nothing shows he forgot anything; giving her white is a deliberate, generous gesture.
Sofia has just helped him; giving her the first move is a welcome, not a wish for her to lose.

items.prompt: Which statement best expresses a theme of the story?
options: Competition between brothers and sisters always damages a family.
Natural talent matters more than practice.
A loss can become a chance to learn and to reconnect with others.
Older brothers and sisters should let younger ones win.
items.explain:
Sofia's loss to Mateo pushed her away from chess and from him. Mateo's loss at the tournament brings them back together: Sofia shares their grandfather's lesson that the best players lose often, asks to learn from Mateo's mistake, and returns to the game. Both losses become starting points for learning and reconnecting.

The story ends with the siblings closer, not damaged. Abuelo's saying about playing “more games than anybody” values practice, and no one in the story lets anyone win.
why: The story ends with the siblings closer, playing together again, so competition did not damage the family.
Abuelo's saying that the best players play "more games than anybody" values practice, not natural talent.
No one in the story lets anyone win; the theme is about learning from losses.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the notice. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“Residents {{0}} leases end on or before June 30 will receive a renewal offer by mail this month.”

options: who's
whose
who
whom
why: "Who's" means "who is"; "Residents who is leases end" makes no sense. Possession needs "whose."
"Who" cannot show possession. The leases belong to the residents, so use "whose."
"Whom" is an object pronoun and cannot show possession.

items.explain:
The leases belong to the residents, so the possessive relative pronoun whose is correct: “Residents whose leases end …”

“Who's” is a contraction of “who is,” which makes no sense here (“who is leases end”). “Who” and “whom” cannot show possession.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the notice. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“Last year, many residents {{0}} their forms after the deadline, which delayed repairs and move-in dates for everyone.”

options: have returned
return
returned
will return
why: The present perfect "have returned" is not used with a specific finished time like "last year." Use the simple past.
"Return" is present tense, but "last year" and "delayed" show a past event.
"Will return" is future tense, but the sentence describes what happened last year.

items.explain:
“Last year” names a specific, finished time in the past, so the simple past tense is correct: returned. The verb “delayed” later in the sentence is also simple past.

The present perfect “have returned” is not used with a specific finished time like “last year.” “Return” (present) and “will return” (future) do not fit a past event.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the notice. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“Beginning April 6, crews will repaint the hallways and replace the carpet on every floor {{0}} the first floor, which was renovated last fall.”

options: accept
expect
except
accepting
why: "Accept" means to receive or agree to. The sentence needs "except," meaning "not including."
"Expect" means to anticipate. The first floor is being left out, so use "except."
"Accepting" means receiving or agreeing to; it does not mean "not including."

items.explain:
Except means “not including.” The first floor is left out because it was already renovated.

“Accept” and “accepting” mean “to receive or agree to,” and “expect” means “to anticipate.” None of them means “not including.”

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the notice. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“The building's water heater is more than twenty years old, and {{0}} efficiency has dropped sharply.”

options: its
it's
its'
their
why: "It's" means "it is"; "it is efficiency" makes no sense. Possessive pronouns have no apostrophe.
"Its'" is not a word. The possessive of "it" is "its."
"Their" is plural, but "water heater" is singular.

items.explain:
The efficiency belongs to the water heater, so the possessive pronoun its is correct. Possessive pronouns never use apostrophes.

“It's” means “it is” (“it is efficiency” makes no sense). “Its'” is not a word. “Their” is plural, but “water heater” is singular.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the notice. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“Because the new heater will be installed on Tuesday, April 14{{0}} water service will be shut off from 9:00 a.m. to 3:00 p.m.”

options: . Water
; water
, water
, and water
why: A period leaves "Because ... April 14" as a fragment. An introductory dependent clause is followed by a comma.
A semicolon joins two independent clauses, but "Because ... April 14" is dependent.
, and wrongly joins a dependent clause to an independent one as if they were equal. Use just a comma.

items.explain:
“Because the new heater will be installed on Tuesday, April 14” is a dependent clause; it cannot stand alone. It must be joined to the main clause, and an introductory dependent clause is followed by a comma: April 14, water service will be shut off.

A period leaves “Because … April 14” as a fragment. A semicolon must join two independent clauses. Adding “and” wrongly links a dependent clause to an independent one as if they were equal.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the notice. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“Neither the maintenance workers nor the building manager {{0}} able to restore water service early, so please plan ahead.”

options: are
is
were
being
why: "Are" agrees with "workers," the farther subject. With neither...nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject, "manager."
"Were" agrees with the farther subject and also shifts to the past tense.
"Being" cannot serve as the main verb of a sentence.

items.explain:
When two subjects are joined by neither … nor, the verb agrees with the subject closer to it. Here the closer subject is “the building manager,” which is singular, so the verb is is.

“Are” and “were” agree with “workers,” the farther subject, and “were” also shifts to the past tense. “Being” cannot serve as the main verb of a sentence.

items.prompt:
Read these sentences from the notice. Choose the transition that best connects them.

“Fill a few containers with water the night before. {{0}}, you may want to run your dishwasher and washing machine before 9:00 a.m.”

options: However
As a result
In addition
Instead
why: "However" signals a contrast, but the second tip adds to the first.
"As a result" signals an effect, but filling containers does not cause anyone to run a dishwasher.
"Instead" signals a replacement, but residents should do both things, not one instead of the other.

items.explain:
Both sentences give advice for preparing for the water shutoff. The second adds another suggestion to the first, so In addition is correct.

“However” and “Instead” signal a contrast or a replacement, but the second tip does not replace the first. “As a result” signals an effect, but filling containers does not cause anyone to run a dishwasher.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the notice. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“Inspectors from the city will visit the building on {{0}} to test every smoke detector.”

options: monday, april 20,
Monday, april 20,
Monday, April 20,
monday, April 20,
why: Days of the week and months are proper nouns; both "Monday" and "April" must be capitalized.
"April" is the name of a month and must be capitalized.
"Monday" is the name of a day and must be capitalized.

items.explain:
Names of days of the week and months of the year are proper nouns and are always capitalized: Monday, April 20,.

Each other choice leaves the day, the month, or both in lowercase.

essay.prompt:
The articles present arguments from a supporter and a critic of starting the high school day later in the morning.

In your response, analyze both positions presented in the articles to determine which one is best supported. Use relevant and specific evidence from both articles to support your response.

Type your response in the box. This task may require approximately 45 minutes to complete.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the email. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“Last year we served more than 4,000 households{{0}} this fall we expect even more.”

options: , this fall
this fall
. This fall
, and, this fall
why: A comma alone between two independent clauses creates a comma splice. Use a period.
No punctuation between two independent clauses creates a run-on sentence.
The comma after "and" is misplaced; a comma goes before the conjunction, not after it.

items.explain:
“Last year we served more than 4,000 households” and “this fall we expect even more” are both independent clauses. A period correctly separates them into two sentences: households. This fall.

A comma alone creates a comma splice, and no punctuation at all creates a run-on. In “, and, this fall,” the comma after “and” is misplaced.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the email. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“There {{0}} several ways to get involved, and every one of them makes a difference.”

options: is
was
are
has been
why: The subject "ways" comes after the verb and is plural, so the verb must be plural: "are."
"Was" is singular and past tense, but "ways" is plural and the email describes current opportunities.
"Has been" is singular; the plural subject "ways" needs "are."

items.explain:
In a sentence that begins with “There,” the subject comes after the verb. The subject here is “ways,” which is plural, so the verb must be plural: There are several ways.

“Is,” “was,” and “has been” are singular. “Was” also shifts to the past, though the email describes current opportunities.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the email. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“Saturday volunteers unload delivery trucks, sort donated food, and {{0}}.”

options: packing grocery boxes for families
pack grocery boxes for families
grocery boxes are packed for families
to pack grocery boxes for families
why: "Packing" breaks the parallel series. The first two items are present-tense verbs, "unload" and "sort," so use "pack."
This switches to a passive clause, breaking the series of active verbs.
"To pack" is an infinitive, which does not match "unload" and "sort."

items.explain:
The first two items in the series are present-tense verbs: “unload” and “sort.” The third must match: pack grocery boxes for families.

“Packing” is an -ing form, “to pack” is an infinitive, and “grocery boxes are packed” is a separate clause in the passive voice, so none of them matches the pattern.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the email. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“On weekday afternoons, volunteers also staff our {{0}} homework table, where students from nearby schools get help with reading and math.”

options: childrens'
childrens
children's
children'
why: "Childrens" is not a word. "Children" is already plural, so add 's: "children's."
"Childrens" is not a word, and the sentence needs a possessive.
"Children'" leaves off the s. An irregular plural that does not end in s takes 's.

items.explain:
“Children” is already plural, and it does not end in s. To make an irregular plural possessive, add an apostrophe and s: children's.

“Childrens” is not a word, so “childrens” and “childrens'” are wrong. “Children'” leaves off the needed s.

items.prompt:
Choose the sentence that is written correctly and belongs in blank (5) of the email.

{{0}}

options: Having helped at the table for three years, the students' progress has amazed me.
Having helped at the table for three years, amazement is what I feel at the students' progress.
Having helped at the table for three years, the progress of the students is amazing.
Having helped at the table for three years, I have been amazed by the students' progress.
why: The word after the comma is "progress," which makes it sound as if the progress helped at the table. This is a dangling modifier.
The word after the comma is "amazement," which could not have helped at the table. The person who helped, "I," must come next.
The word after the comma is "progress," so the modifier dangles. Name the helper, "I," right after the comma.

items.explain:
The introductory phrase “Having helped at the table for three years” describes a person, so the word right after the comma must name the person who helped: I. “Having helped at the table for three years, I have been amazed by the students' progress” is correct.

In the other choices, the word after the comma is “progress” or “amazement,” which makes it sound as if progress or amazement helped at the table. These are dangling modifiers.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the email. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“Many students who started the year behind in reading now do {{0}} on their weekly quizzes.”

options: good
real good
more good
well
why: "Good" is an adjective and cannot describe the verb "do." Use the adverb "well."
"Real good" adds a second error; "do" needs the adverb "well."
"More good" is not standard English. The adverb "well" describes how they do.

items.explain:
The blank describes how the students do, which is an action verb, so it needs an adverb: well.

“Good” is an adjective and cannot describe the verb “do.” “Real good” adds a second error (“real” should be “really”), and “more good” is not standard English.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the email. Choose the option that completes it most clearly and correctly.

“{{0}} you do not need any experience to volunteer.”

options: Due to the fact that full training is provided to all volunteers by us, it is the case that
We provide full training, therefore,
Because we provide full training,
Because of the fact that we provide full training in advance before you begin,
why: This is wordy and roundabout. "Because we provide full training," says the same thing clearly.
"Therefore" cannot join two independent clauses with only commas; this creates a comma splice.
This is wordy and repetitive: "in advance" and "before you begin" mean the same thing.

items.explain:
Because we provide full training, states the reason clearly, in as few words as possible, and correctly joins a dependent clause to the main clause.

“Due to the fact that … it is the case that” and “Because of the fact that … in advance before you begin” are wordy and repetitive (“in advance” and “before you begin” mean the same thing). “We provide full training, therefore,” creates a comma splice, because “therefore” cannot join two independent clauses with only commas.

items.prompt:
Read this sentence from the email. Choose the option that correctly completes it.

“If you have questions about which role fits you best, I would be glad to {{0}} you.”

options: advise
advice
advising
advices
why: "Advice" is a noun. After "to," the sentence needs the verb "advise."
After "to," use the base form of the verb, "advise," not "advising."
"Advices" is not standard, and the sentence needs a verb, not a noun.

items.explain:
Advise is the verb meaning “to give guidance.” After “to,” the base form of the verb is needed: “glad to advise you.”

“Advice” is a noun (“some advice”), and “advices” is not standard. “Advising” is the wrong form to follow “to.”

items.prompt: Which statement best expresses the central idea of “Cities Built by Animals”?
options: Coral reefs are made of rock, even though they look like living gardens.
The Great Barrier Reef is the largest and most important reef in the world.
Overfishing is now the greatest threat to coral reefs.
Reefs are rich, valuable structures built by a partnership between corals and algae, and rising ocean temperatures and other stresses now threaten that partnership.
items.explain:
The passage explains how polyps build reefs (paragraph 2) with the help of algae (paragraph 3), why reefs matter (paragraph 4), how heat breaks the partnership through bleaching (paragraphs 5–6), and what other threats exist (paragraph 7). It ends by saying reef survival depends on slowing ocean warming.

The claim that reefs are simply rock reverses paragraph 1, which says a reef is built by living animals. The Great Barrier Reef is one example. Overfishing is one of several threats, and the passage treats heat as the larger one.
why: This reverses paragraph 1, which says a reef is built by living animals, not simply rock.
The Great Barrier Reef is one example in paragraph 6, not the subject of the whole passage.
Overfishing is one of several threats in paragraph 7; the passage treats ocean warming as the larger one.

items.prompt: What is the main purpose of paragraph 1?
options: to contrast how a reef looks from a distance with what it actually is
to argue that reefs should be protected in the same way as gardens
to describe what divers experience when they explore a reef
to explain why the rocks on a reef are so colorful
items.explain:
Paragraph 1 says that from a boat a reef “can look like a garden of colorful rocks,” but “up close, it is something stranger: a structure built … by animals.” It contrasts appearance with reality and sets up the explanation of polyps in paragraph 2.

The paragraph makes no argument about protection, does not describe diving, and the source of the colors (the algae) is explained in paragraph 3.
why: Paragraph 1 makes no argument about protecting reefs.
Paragraph 1 describes the view from a boat, not divers exploring a reef.
The source of the colors, the algae, is explained in paragraph 3, not paragraph 1.

items.prompt: According to paragraph 5, in what order do these events happen when a coral bleaches and does not recover? Drag each event into the correct position.
choices: The coral's white skeleton shows through its nearly clear tissue.
Water stays warmer than the usual summer maximum for several weeks.
The coral dies, and seaweed may cover its skeleton.
The stressed coral expels its algae.
items.explain: (1) The water stays about 1 °C above the usual summer maximum for several weeks. (2) The stressed corals “expel their algae.” (3) “Without the algae,” the tissue becomes nearly transparent and the white skeleton shows through (bleaching). (4) “If the heat lasts too long, the coral dies, and seaweed may soon cover its skeleton.”
items.why: The most common error is placing "expels its algae" after the white skeleton shows through. Paragraph 5 says the stressed coral expels its algae first, and only "without the algae" does the skeleton show through.

items.prompt: As it is used in paragraph 5, the word expel most nearly means—
options: take in
feed
force out
hide
items.explain:
The next sentence begins, “Without the algae,” so after the corals expel them, the algae are gone. To expel is to force out.

“Take in” is the opposite. “Feed” and “hide” would not leave the coral without its algae.
why: "Take in" is the opposite. The next sentence begins "Without the algae," so the algae have been forced out.
Feeding the algae would not leave the coral "without the algae."
Hiding the algae would not make the tissue transparent; the algae are gone, so expel means force out.

items.prompt: According to paragraph 3, why do most coral reefs grow in shallow, clear water?
options: Waves in shallow water bring polyps the minerals they need.
The algae living inside the corals need sunlight to make food.
Fish that feed on reefs cannot swim in deep water.
Deep water is too warm for corals to survive.
items.explain:
Paragraph 3 says, “Because the algae depend on sunlight, most reefs grow in shallow, clear water.” The algae make food through photosynthesis, and the coral depends on that food.

The passage does not connect waves to minerals or say that fish cannot swim deep. Deep water is not described as too warm; heat is a problem at the surface.
why: Paragraph 3 says nothing about waves and minerals; it ties shallow water to the algae's need for sunlight.
The passage never says fish cannot swim in deep water.
The passage does not call deep water too warm; heat is a problem near the surface.

items.prompt: Paragraph 7 is shown below. Click the sentence that explains how a decrease in the number of fish can harm a reef.
spans: Heat is not the only threat.
Pollution running off the land clouds the water and blocks sunlight.
Overfishing removes fish that graze on seaweed, allowing it to crowd out young corals.
And as the ocean absorbs carbon dioxide from the air, seawater becomes slightly more acidic, which makes it harder for corals to build their skeletons.
items.explain:
When overfishing removes fish that eat seaweed, the seaweed grows unchecked and can “crowd out young corals.” That is the chain of cause and effect linking fewer fish to reef damage.

The pollution and acidity sentences describe other threats that do not involve fish.
items.why: The most common wrong click is the pollution sentence, which describes a threat that does not involve fish. The overfishing sentence links fewer seaweed-eating fish to seaweed crowding out young corals.

items.prompt: Based on paragraphs 5 and 6, why is the increasing frequency of mass bleaching events especially harmful to reefs?
options: Every coral that bleaches dies within a few days.
Mass bleaching events affect only the Great Barrier Reef.
Bleached corals spread disease to the fish that live around them.
Corals that might recover from one event have less time to do so before the next.
items.explain:
Paragraph 5 explains that a bleached coral “is not dead” and can recover “if temperatures return to normal soon enough.” Paragraph 6 says mass bleaching now happens “often enough that many reefs have little time to recover between them.” Frequent events take away the recovery time that bleached corals need.

The claim that every bleached coral dies within days contradicts paragraph 5. The Great Barrier Reef is an example, not the only reef affected. Disease spreading to fish is never mentioned.
why: Paragraph 5 says a bleached coral "is not dead" and can recover if temperatures return to normal soon enough.
The Great Barrier Reef is given as an example; paragraph 6 says many reefs have little time to recover.
The passage never says bleached corals spread disease to fish.

items.prompt: In paragraph 4, why does the author point out that reefs cover less than 1 percent of the ocean floor but support about a quarter of all known marine species?
options: to emphasize how much life reefs support for their small size
to show that most marine species are in danger of extinction
to argue that reefs should be expanded to cover more of the ocean floor
to explain how reefs are able to slow waves before they reach shore
items.explain:
The paragraph opens by calling reefs “among the richest habitats on Earth.” Setting a very small area (less than 1 percent) beside a very large share of species (about a quarter) shows just how rich they are.

The statistic says nothing about extinction, the author never proposes expanding reefs, and the breakwater point comes later in the paragraph and has nothing to do with species.
why: The statistic shows how rich reefs are; it says nothing about extinction.
The author never proposes expanding reefs.
Slowing waves is a separate point later in paragraph 4 and has nothing to do with the number of species.

items.prompt: According to the table in “Can We Replant a Reef?”, during which period did the greatest number of outplanted fragments die?
options: between outplanting and the end of year 1
between the end of year 1 and the end of year 2
between the end of year 2 and the end of year 3
between the end of year 3 and the end of year 4
items.explain:
Find the number lost in each period:

Outplanting to year 1: 1,000 − 820 = 180
Year 1 to year 2: 820 − 710 = 110
Year 2 to year 3: 710 − 290 = 420
Year 3 to year 4: 290 − 260 = 30

The largest loss, 420 fragments, came between years 2 and 3, the year the table notes a marine heat wave.
why: The first year lost 1,000 − 820 = 180 fragments, fewer than the 420 lost in year 3.
Year 1 to year 2 lost 820 − 710 = 110 fragments.
Year 3 to year 4 lost only 290 − 260 = 30 fragments. Year 3 had the lowest survivors, but the biggest loss came during the heat wave year.

items.skill: Drawing conclusions from text and data
items.prompt: Which conclusion is best supported by both the table and paragraph 4 of “Can We Replant a Reef?”
options: Outplanted corals rarely survive their first year.
A single marine heat wave can undo much of a restoration project's progress.
Restoration projects have replaced most of the coral that reefs have lost.
The sample project used only heat-tolerant corals.
items.explain:
Paragraph 4 warns that “a single severe marine heat wave can wipe out much of a nursery's work.” The table shows exactly that: survival fell from 71% to 29% in the year of the heat wave, a loss of 420 of the 710 surviving fragments.

82% survived the first year, so they did not “rarely survive.” Paragraph 4 says projects have replanted “only a tiny fraction” of lost reef. The passage never says which corals the sample project used.
why: The table shows 82% survived the first year, so they did not rarely survive.
Paragraph 4 says projects have replanted "only a tiny fraction" of lost reef.
The passage never says which corals the sample project used.

items.prompt: Which ideas appear in both “Cities Built by Animals” and “Can We Replant a Reef?” Select two answers.
options: Unusually warm water can kill corals.
The long-term survival of reefs depends on addressing ocean warming.
Coral fragments can be grown in underwater nurseries.
Reefs protect coastal towns from storm damage.
Some coral colonies tolerate heat better than others.
Reefs support about a quarter of all known marine species.
items.explain:
Warm water kills coral: “Cities Built by Animals” says that if the heat lasts too long, “the coral dies” (paragraph 5); “Can We Replant a Reef?” says a marine heat wave can “wipe out much of a nursery's work” (paragraph 4), and the table shows it.

Ocean warming must be addressed: the first passage ends by saying survival “depends on slowing the warming of the oceans themselves” (paragraph 8); the second compares restoration without that action to mopping while the sink overflows and calls slowing ocean warming part of “the larger work” (paragraphs 4 and 6).

Nurseries and heat-tolerant colonies appear only in the second passage. Storm protection and the quarter of marine species appear only in the first.
why: Coral nurseries appear only in "Can We Replant a Reef?"
Storm protection appears only in "Cities Built by Animals" (paragraph 4).
Heat-tolerant colonies appear only in "Can We Replant a Reef?" (paragraph 3).
The quarter of marine species appears only in "Cities Built by Animals."

items.prompt: In paragraph 4, critics compare restoration without action on ocean warming to “mopping the floor while the sink is still overflowing.” What point does this comparison make?
options: Restoration teams need to work faster to keep up with the damage.
Restoration is useless and should be stopped.
Restoration is simple work that volunteers can do as easily as household chores.
Repairing damage cannot succeed for long unless the cause of the damage is also addressed.
items.explain:
Mopping cleans up the water on the floor, but as long as the sink overflows, more water keeps coming. In the same way, replanting coral repairs damage, but warming water keeps causing new damage. The critics' point is that the cause, ocean warming, must also be addressed.

The paragraph opens by saying critics “do not argue that restoration is useless,” which rules out the claim that restoration is useless and should be stopped. The comparison is not about speed or about how easy the work is.
why: The comparison is not about speed. Mopping faster still cannot keep up while the sink overflows; the source must be stopped.
Paragraph 4 opens by saying critics "do not argue that restoration is useless."
The comparison is not about how easy the work is; it is about fixing the cause of the damage.

items.prompt: Which statement best describes the author's own view of coral restoration in “Can We Replant a Reef?”
options: Restoration is a useful but limited tool that works best alongside efforts to address the causes of reef decline.
Restoration has already proved that reefs can recover without any change in ocean temperatures.
Restoration wastes money that should be spent on reducing pollution instead.
Restoration is the single most important way to protect the world's reefs.
items.explain:
The author presents both supporters (paragraph 3) and critics (paragraph 4), says the sample project “shows both sides of the debate” (paragraph 5), and concludes that restoration is “one tool among several: a way to buy time for reefs while the larger work … goes on” (paragraph 6).

The table shows heat wiping out most fragments, which contradicts the claim that reefs have recovered without any change in ocean temperatures. The author never calls restoration a waste of money, and calling it “one tool among several” rules out “the single most important way.”
why: The table shows a heat wave wiping out most fragments, which contradicts recovery without any change in ocean temperatures.
The author never calls restoration a waste of money; paragraph 6 calls it a useful tool.
Paragraph 6 calls restoration "one tool among several," not the single most important way.
